related-article.article-title: Transient acute neuronal activation response caused by high concentrations of oligonucleotides in the cerebral spinal fluid

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are an important therapeutic modality for neurological diseases. Some ASOs cause transient neurobehavioral responses acutely following intrathecal delivery to the central nervous system (CNS). We characterized a subset of these responses, including hypoactivity, spinal reflex loss, paresis, sedation, and ataxia, that are suggestive of neuronal inhibition in rodents and non-human primates. Across species, inhibition-like responses peaked ∼3 h post-ASO delivery, reversed within 24 h with no sequelae, and could be quantified using simple neurobehavioral scales. Acute inhibition was dose-responsive and was abrogated with lower phosphorothioate and guanine content in ASOs. Acutely inhibitory ASOs transiently disrupted motor pathway neurotransmission in vivo and suppressed firing in primary neural cultures. In vitro firing rate suppression of >60% predicted high in vivo acute inhibition scores and was reversed immediately with addition of varying excitatory agents or upon ASO washout. Peak acute inhibition in vivo coincided with peak CNS tissue concentrations of ASO and abated as ASO was internalized by parenchymal cells and cleared from the extracellular space. We propose transient high extracellular concentrations block synaptic transmission via non-specific protein binding of phosphorothioate ASOs. Our results define a comprehensive framework for quantifying and mitigating ASO-mediated acute inhibition.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are synthetic strands of nucleotides typically 12–30 bases in length that can be designed to hybridize to RNA and modulate gene expression via several different mechanisms [1]. Two ASO therapeutics delivered directly to the central nervous system (CNS) have been approved for neurological disorders: nusinersen (Spinraza) for spinal muscular atrophy and tofersen (Qalsody) for superoxide dismutase 1-amyotrophic lateral sclerosis [2–4]. Because ASOs can selectively target RNA at the underlying cause of disease, they hold promise as disease-modifying treatments in a broad range of neurological disorders. Many CNS-targeted ASO therapies are now in clinical development [5–9].

ASOs are relatively large, highly charged molecules that do not cross the blood–brain barrier and are instead administered to the CNS by intrathecal (IT) bolus into the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) [10]. The ASO then distributes up the neuraxis and penetrates into CNS tissues in the minutes to hours after injection, resulting in transient, high local concentrations of ASO in the intrathecal space surrounding the spinal cord and nerve roots and in the extracellular space of the CNS parenchyma before it is taken up into cells and excess is cleared into the periphery [11, 12]. Hybridization-independent effects of phosphorothioate oligonucleotides, including interactions with a broad range of proteins, have been reported [13–16]. Given the high local concentrations and tendency for ASOs to interact with many proteins, it is not surprising that certain ASOs cause transient neurobehavioral responses in rodents and non-human primates (NHP) during the distribution phase acutely following IT administration [17–21].

The neurobehavioral responses observed with some ASOs include those indicative of nervous system inhibition, including decreased spinal reflexes, motor activity, and muscle strength, as well as ataxia, decreased consciousness, slowed breathing, and abnormal posture [17–21]. Also described are responses of ASOs and other oligonucleotide classes suggestive of nervous system activation, including increased locomotor activity, nystagmus, stereotypy, muscle tremors, spasticity, convulsions, and seizures [18, 21]. We hypothesize these two different responses (acute activation and acute inhibition) are mechanistically distinct, because though they both happen shortly after IT delivery of oligonucleotides, the presentation suggests differential effects on the CNS [17–21].

Here, we aimed to carefully characterize and classify the distinct acute inhibition response following ASO administration into the CNS. We demonstrate that acute inhibition is dose-, sequence-, and chemistry-dependent. It can be captured in a neurobehavioral scale and translates across preclinical species, including mice, rats, and NHP. It can be modeled in an in vitro screening assay that is predictive of the in vivo response. We show the acute inhibition response is due to high extracellular concentrations of ASO occurring during the initial distribution phase, which transiently inhibits synaptic transmission prior to CNS intracellular uptake and extracellular clearance of ASO into systemic circulation. This is mechanistically distinct from the acute activation response, which is characterized in our companion manuscript [22].

sec.title: ASO preparation
sec.p: Lyophilized ASOs (Supplementary Tables S1–S3) were dissolved in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) without Ca2+ or Mg2+ for all studies, unless otherwise noted. For dosing solutions containing supplemental Ca2+ or Mg2+, CaCl2 and MgCl2 stock solutions were formulated in aCSF. ASOs were quantified by UV spectrometry and sterilized by passage through a 0.2-µm sterile filter before dosing.

sec.title: Intracerebroventricular administration in rodents
sec.p: All protocols met ethical standards for animal experimentation and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of Ionis Pharmaceuticals. Female C57BL/6J mice were obtained from the Jackson Laboratory (stock # 000664; Bar Harbor, ME). Intracerebroventricular (ICV) injections in mice were performed as previously described [11]. Briefly, animals were anesthetized with isoflurane and placed in a stereotaxic frame, and an incision was made in the scalp. A Hamilton microsyringe was placed at 0.3 mm anterior and 1.0 mm lateral to bregma and was lowered 3.0 mm into the lateral ventricle. A 10 μl volume of ASO solution was injected at a rate of 1 μl/s, and the needle was held in place for 3 min before being withdrawn.

Male Sprague-Dawley rats with body weights between 0.25 and 0.4 kg were obtained from Harlan Laboratories (stock # 213M, Livermore, CA). For ICV injections in rats, animals were anesthetized with isoflurane and placed in a stereotaxic frame, and an incision was made in the scalp. A hole was drilled 1 mm posterior and 1.5 mm lateral to bregma. A Hamilton microsyringe was then placed at the hole and lowered 3.7 mm into the lateral ventricle. A 30 μl volume of ASO solution was injected at a rate of 1 μl/s, and the needle was held in place for 3 min before being withdrawn.

sec.title: Intrathecal administration in rats
sec.p: IT administration of ASO in rats was performed under a protocol approved by the IACUC of Ionis Pharmaceuticals. Male Sprague-Dawley rats with body weights between 0.25 and 0.4 kg were obtained from Harlan Laboratories (stock # 213M, Livermore, CA). Catheterization of the lumbar intrathecal space was performed as described previously [23]. ASO or vehicle was delivered over 30 s in a 30 μl volume followed by a flush of 40 μl vehicle.

sec.title: Intrathecal administration of ASO in NHP
sec.p: NHP studies were performed at Northern Biomedical Research, Inc., Spring Lake, MI, and were approved by their IACUC. As previously described [11], adult male or female cynomolgus monkeys were anesthetized, and 1 ml aCSF or ASO dosing solution in aCSF was administered via percutaneous IT injection over 1 min using a spinal needle at the lumbar level (target L4/L5 space). Animals were dosed in lateral recumbency position and remained in a prone position for at least 15 min following dosing.

sec.title: Acute inhibition scoring following IT administration in rodents
sec.p: Animals are lifted out of their home cages and observed on a flat surface 3 h after ASO IT administration. They are assessed according to the scale in Supplementary Fig. S1A. Scores are as follows. 0 = bright, alert, responsive. 1 = the tail hits the table surface without tone when gently lifted to hip level. 2 = the hind end is drooping, or abnormal gait is present in hindlimbs. 3 = hind limbs are unable to support weight, but hind paws can still move. 4 = hind limbs and hind paws are not moving at all. 5 = the animal is unable to support its anterior body weight with forelimbs. 6 = the animal cannot move its forelimbs, but there is some movement, including breathing. Death is scored as a 7.

sec.title: Acute inhibition scoring following ICV administration in rodents
sec.p: Animals are observed in their home cages 3 h after ASO ICV injection. They are assessed according to the scale in Supplementary Fig. S1B. The scores are as follows. 0 = bright, alert, and responsive. 1 = mild gait impairment (i.e. wobbly walking). 2 = obvious impaired gait and/or a hunched posture. If the animal is lying on its side and is not ambulating in the home cage, it is then lifted out and placed on a flat surface. 3 = moves away from the experimenter after lifting. 4 = does not move forward after lifting but has an upright posture. 5 = lying on its side and does not move after lift but responds to tail pinch. 6 = does not respond to pinch but is breathing. Death is scored as a 7.

sec.title: Acute spinal reflex scoring following IT administration in NHP
sec.p: Lower spinal reflexes and general motor function are assessed as a part of standard neurological examinations 2–4 h after IT administration of ASO in NHP, and scores are derived post-hoc from the reports according to the scale in Supplementary Fig. S1C. For each reflex assessed, a lack of response to stimulus is given a score of 1; response to stimulus is given a score of 0. A cumulative score is assigned for each animal. Tail reflex: when the tail is touched with a sharp object, the tail should move to avoid the stimulus. Cutaneous reflex: the reaction to a series of needle pricks along each side of the abdomen is recorded. Sensory foot reflex: the foot is stimulated with a sharp object and an avoidance response is observed. Proprioceptive reflex: each foot is inverted, and the ability to right the foot is noted. Knee jerk reflex: the presence or absence of a quick extension of a hind leg is noted following the tapping of the patellar ligament with a reflex hammer.

sec.title: In vivo electrophysiological recordings
sec.p: Electrophysiological recordings were performed in rats to assess function of motor and sensory pathways as previously reported: myogenic motor-evoked potentials (MMEPs) [24], spinal surface motor-evoked potentials (SMEPs) [25], spinal surface somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) [26], and Hoffman reflex (HR) [27]. Briefly, animals were anesthetized with propofol (50–100 mg/kg, i.p.) for MMEPs or isoflurane [2.0%–2.5% (vol/vol) maintenance; in room air] for all other surgical procedures and electrophysiological recordings. Rats were instrumented with electrodes for stimulation overlying the left and right motor cortex or tibial nerve and for recordings in the thoracic spinal cord, lumbar spinal cord, or peripheral muscle. After electrode placement, animals were injected with ketamine propofol (50–100 mg/kg, i.p.). For each round of recordings, the animals first received vehicle via IT administration to measure a baseline recording, then received an ASO. Electrophysiological recordings were taken 2 and 24 h after ASO administration. Evoked potentials were generated using a DS3 constant-current isolated stimulator (Digitimer). Recording electrodes were connected to an active head stage (3110W head stage; Warner Instruments) and signal-amplified (×100 times) using DP-311 differential amplifier (Warner Instruments). Amplified signal was acquired by the PowerLab 8/30 data-acquisition system (ADInstruments) at sampling frequency of 20 kHz, digitized, and stored in PC for analysis.

MMEPs were elicited by transcranial electrical stimulation of the motor cortex using 30-G stainless-steel stimulating electrodes with a pulse duration of 1 ms at 7.5 mA. Responses were recorded from the gastrocnemius muscle using 30-G platinum transcutaneous needle electrodes (distance between recording electrodes ∼1 cm; Grass Technologies, Astro-Med).

SMEPs were elicited by transcranial electrical stimulation of the motor cortex as above with a pulse duration of 0.2 ms at 7.0 mA. Evoked responses were recorded by a pair of flexible silver-ball electrodes on the dura surface of the exposed T12 spinal segment (distance between recording electrodes ∼0.5 cm). A reference silver-chloride disk electrode was located subcutaneously on the contralateral side of the recording.

SSEPs were elicited using two 30-G stainless-steel stimulating electrodes transcutaneously inserted into the surroundings of the tibial nerve (distance between stimulation electrodes ∼1 cm; Grass Technologies, Astro-Med) with a pulse duration of 0.2 ms at 6.0 mA. Evoked responses were recorded by a pair of flexible silver-ball electrodes placed on the dura surface of the exposed L2–L5 spinal segment (distance between recording electrodes ∼0.5 cm). A reference silver-chloride disk electrode was located subcutaneously on the contralateral side of the recording.

HR was elicited using stimulating needle electrodes transcutaneously inserted into the surroundings of the tibial nerve. Responses were recorded through a pair of 30-G platinum needle electrodes inserted into the interosseous muscles between the fourth and the fifth, or the first and the second metatarsal muscles of the right hind paw, and a grounding electrode was placed into the tail. The tibial nerve was stimulated using square pulses with increasing stimulus intensity (0.1–10 mA in 0.5-mA increments, 0.1 Hz, 0.2 ms). We used these data to determine the intensity necessary to obtain a maximal M and H response.

sec.title: Tissue harvesting
sec.p: Mice and rats were euthanized 1 h to 2 weeks after the ASO injection, as indicated for each study. Frozen brain and spinal cord tissues were harvested for the determination of ASO concentration and target messenger RNA expression as described below. Tissues were also immersion-fixed in 10% buffered formalin solution for histological processing as described below.

sec.title: Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction
sec.p: RNA was extracted, and qRT-PCR performed as previously described [11] using gene-specific primers (IDT Technologies, Coralville, IA). For Malat1-targeted ASO5-treated mice, the expression level of Malat1 was normalized to that of Gapdh, and this was further normalized to the level in vehicle treated animals. Primer/probes sequences: Malat1 forward – AGGCGGGCAGCTAAGGA; Malat1 reverse – CCCCACTGTAGCATCACATCA; Malat1 probe – TTCCTCTGCCGGTCCCTCGAAAG; Gapdh forward – GGCAAATTCAACGGCACAGT; Gapdh reverse – GGGTCTCGCTCCTGGAAGAT; Gapdh probe – AAGGCCGAGAATGGGAAGCTTGTCATC.

sec.title: Quantification of ASO tissue levels
sec.p: ASO6 and ASO6_PO were quantified in rat CNS tissue as previously described [28]. Briefly, ASO was extracted from tissues via liquid–liquid extraction. The aqueous layer was processed via solid-phase extraction with a Strata X plate. Eluates were passed through a protein-precipitation plate before drying down under nitrogen at 50°C. Dried samples were reconstituted in 140 μl water containing 100 μM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid and were run on an Agilent 6130B single quadrupole LCMS to quantify ASO concentration.

sec.title: Generation of mouse primary cortical cultures and multielectrode array recordings
sec.p: Mouse cortical cells were isolated from C57BL/6 embryos on day 16 and plated in multielectrode array (MEA) plates pre-coated with poly-D-lysine at 150 K to 200 K per well and cultured in Neurobasal media. Neurons were cultured for 2 weeks on 24-well glass-bottom plates from Multi Channel Systems containing 12 electrodes. For MEA recordings, a 10-min baseline activity was recorded for all wells. Then cultures were treated with ASO at concentrations from 5 to 150 µM and recorded for an additional 10 min. For washout experiments, after recording the ASO treatment phase, wells were washed 2× with media to remove ASO before recording again. Percent inhibition was calculated as 100% X (1-Spike Rate (ASO)/Spike Rate (baseline)) and if Spike Rate ASO > Spike Rate baseline percent inhibition was recorded as 0.

sec.title: Histology
sec.p: Rat brains were processed as described previously [11]. Briefly, they were bisected sagittally at the midline, immersion-fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin (Statlab, 28600-1) for 72 h, transferred to 70% ethanol, processed into Paraplast Plus paraffin (Leica, 39602004) overnight on a Sakura Tissue-Tek tissue processor, and embedded in paraffin. Tissue sections were cut at 4 μm thick and mounted on positively charged slides (Millennia 1000, Statlab, M1000W), then air-dried overnight and dried at 60°C in a slide drying oven for 1 h prior to staining.

sec.title: ASO immunohistochemistry
sec.p: Slides were stained with rabbit polyclonal anti-ASO antibody (Ionis) on a Ventana Ultra staining system. ASO slides were treated enzymatically with trypsin (Sigma, T8003). The slides were then blocked with Endogenous Biotin Blocking Kit (Ventana, 760-050) and Normal Goat Serum (Jackson Immuno Labs, 005-000-121). The primary antibody was diluted with Discovery Antibody Diluent (Ventana, 760-108) and incubated for 1 h at 37°C. The antibodies were detected with biotin-labeled goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (Jackson Immuno Labs, 111-005-003). The secondary antibody was labeled with DABMap Kit (Ventana, 760-124). Note: ASO antibody staining level is dependent on ASO sequence and phosphorothioate (PS) content in the backbone. Images were scanned on a Hamamatsu S360 scanner at 20× resolution.

sec.title: Data analysis
sec.p: All data are shown as mean ± SD, and all analyses were conducted using Prism software (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA). Grip strength and open field statistical analysis were determined by two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). Acute inhibition score graphs were determined by nonparametric tests such as Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn’s multiple comparison or Mann–Whitney and stated in the figure legends. Correlation graphs were determined by Spearman r test. ED50s were determined by non-linear regression with normalized response and variable slope (Motulsky). For specific tests, number of animals or samples per treatment group, and P values, see Supplementary Tables S4–S22.

sec.title: Acute inhibition is transient, reversible, and dose-dependent following CNS ASO administration
sec.p: In pharmacology screening studies, we observed that certain ASOs caused transient loss of muscle strength and paresis/paralysis following IT administration. To better characterize the response, we administered ASO1 in dose response and assessed motor behavior over time (Fig. 1A). Muscle weakness/paresis was present in posterior regions at 30–300 µg doses. At higher doses of 700–1000 µg, both posterior and anterior regions were impacted. At 1-h post-dose, paresis was present in posterior regions and moved progressively anterior with time, with the response peaking at 3–4 h. Paresis/paralysis began to wane between 5 and 8 h, wearing off in an anterior-to-posterior pattern.

caption.p: ASO-mediated acute inhibition response is transient, reversible, and dose- and concentration-dependent. (A) Wild-type rats were dosed with vehicle (saline) or 100, 300, 700, or 1000 µg of ASO1 via IT administration and assessed for motor function at 1–8 h and at 24 h post-dose. The heatmap shows the number of rats/group that exhibited paresis/paralysis in the designated regions over time (white = 0/4; green = 4/4). (B) Time course of acute inhibition as scored on the scale developed for IT administration in rodents. Rats received 700 µg of ASO1. (C) Acute inhibition as scored on the scale developed for ICV bolus injections in rats at 3 h post-ICV delivery of 700 µg of ASO1. (D) Comparison of ASO tissue concentrations across CNS regions following ICV (orange) or IT (green) administration of 700 µg ASO1. Statistical analysis in panel (D), ASO concentrations are relative to the anterior cortex. The specific number of animals per group and P values are included in the corresponding supplementary tables (Supplementary Table S4–S6). *P < .05, **P < .01, ***P < .001, ****P < .0001. T = Tail; PP = posterior posture; HL = hind limbs; HP = hind paws, AP = anterior posture, FP = forepaws, CX = cortex, and SC = spinal cord. .

sec.p: We adapted these observations into a scale to capture the level of acute inhibition after IT delivery of various ASOs in rodents (Supplementary Fig. S1A). The scale gives one point for the presence of paresis/paralysis in seven regions depicted in the cartoon in Fig. 1B. Acute inhibition response scores were assessed at 30 min to 2 weeks after 700 µg of ASO1 delivered via IT administration in rats (Fig. 1B). At 30 min post-dose, all animals exhibited a score of 1 (tail paralysis). By 3 h, peak scores of 4 were reached (full tail, hindlimb, and hind paw paralysis). By 16–24 h and for the next 2 weeks, all animals scored a 0, confirming acute inhibition is transient with no long-term sequelae. For subsequent studies, we focused on the time of the peak acute inhibition response at 3 h post-dosing.

Since acute inhibition presented in a dose-dependent and posterior-to-anterior pattern, we hypothesized the response was due to a posterior-to-anterior ASO concentration gradient in CNS tissues in the hours after IT administration. This is consistent with the previously published gradient that occurs as ASO distributes up the neuraxis [12]. To test this hypothesis, we delivered 700 µg ASO1 via IT (Fig. 1B) or via intracerebroventricular (ICV) injection and compared the neurobehavioral responses and concentrations of ASO across CNS regions 3 h post-dose. Via ICV injection, ASO1 caused a general sedation more consistent with inhibition of brain function than spinal cord function. We translated these observations into a similar 7-point scoring system for quantification of acute inhibition response after ICV in rodents (Fig. 1C and Supplementary Fig. S1B). Tissue concentrations of ASO1 were highest in the posterior spinal cord and lowest in the anterior cortex following IT administration, consistent with the posterior paralysis observed (Fig. 1B and D). In contrast, ASO1 tissue concentrations were higher in the brain and lower in the spinal cord after ICV injection, indicating CNS regions with the highest concentrations are most affected by the acute inhibition response (Fig. 1D).

sec.title: Acute inhibition response is sequence-dependent
sec.p: We next delivered ASO1 by ICV injection in mice and found a similar neurobehavioral response to that in rats, as assessed by the rodent ICV acute inhibition scale (Supplementary Fig. S2A). To determine the sequence dependence of the acute inhibition response, we selected a panel of seven ASOs with different nucleotide sequences but identical chemistries—fully phosphorothioate (PS) modified 20-mer oligonucleotides with a 10-base deoxynucleotide gap flanked on each end with 5 2′-O-Methoxyethyl (MOE) modified nucleotides (ASOs 2–8; Supplementary Table S1). Following a single 100 µg ICV injection in mice, the acute inhibition response at 3 h post-injection varied from 0 to 5, depending upon the sequence tested (Fig. 2A), and resolved by 24 h. To further characterize the dose-dependency of the response in mice, we administered ASO5 from 30 to 700 µg via ICV injection and found acute inhibition scores significantly increased with dose level (Fig. 2B). To test the relevancy of our scale to well-established, sensitive locomotor behavior assays, we assessed grip strength [29] and open field [30] in these animals (Supplementary Fig. S2B–E), the scores for which were significantly correlated to acute inhibition scores (Supplementary Fig. S2F and G).

caption.p: ASO-mediated acute inhibition responses are sequence dependent. (A) Acute inhibition scores in mice at 3 h post-injection of ASO2–8 (100 µg) compared to PBS controls using the rodent ICV acute inhibition scale (0–7). (B) Acute inhibition scores in mice following increasing doses (30, 100, 300, and 700 µg) of ASO5 compared to PBS controls and scored at 3 h post-ICV dose. (C) Total number of guanines (Gs) in a given ASO sequence compared to the 3 h acute inhibition score following 700 µg ICV injection in mice. (D) Total number of cytosines (Cs) in a given ASO sequence compared to the 3 h acute inhibition score following 700 µg ICV injection in mice. See Supplementary Tables S7–S9 for statistical analysis. *P < .05, **P < .01, ***P < .001, ****P < .0001.

sec.title: G-rich, C-poor sequences result in more severe acute inhibition
sec.p: ASO sequences enriched for guanine (G) nucleotides, particularly at the 3′ end of the ASO, were previously associated with suppression of synchronous neuronal activity in an in vitro model of ASO toxicity, while conversely adenine (A)-rich sequences were associated with maintenance of neuronal activity [19]. To expand on this finding in an in vivo setting, we compared the nucleotide content and placement in ∼1800 ASOs to their in vivo acute inhibition scores and found the severity of acute inhibition to be positively associated with enrichment for G nucleotides (Fig. 2C), whether in the DNA gap or the 2′-MOE wings (Supplementary Fig. S3B). Furthermore, we found high cytosine (C) content and adenosine (A) content were associated with a trend in low acute inhibition scores, while thymine (T)-rich sequences bore no specific effect on severity of acute inhibition (Fig. 2D and Supplementary Fig. S3A). This data indicates sequence features can profoundly affect acute inhibition, with G and C having opposing effects.

sec.title: Acute inhibition response translates across species
sec.p: To determine how well the acute inhibition response translates across preclinical models, we compared the acute inhibition scores of over 1000 ASOs that were tested in both mice and rats. Acute inhibition scores were highly correlated (Spearman ρ = 0.67, Fig. 3A), indicating acutely inhibitory ASOs can be identified in mice or rats, regardless of administration route or scale used.

caption.p: ASO-mediated acute inhibition responses translate across preclinical species and are dose dependent. (A) Correlation plots of acute inhibition scores for different ASOs 3 h post-dosing in rat (3000 µg IT) and mouse (700 µg ICV). (B) Dose-dependent acute inhibition scores observed with ASO6 in mice, rats, and NHPs (2–4 h post-dosing). The specific number per group and P value are included in Supplementary Tables S10 and S11. Each data point represents individual animals’ scores. *P < .05, **P < .01, ***P < .001, ****P < .0001 using the nonparametric Kruskal–Wallis test and Dunn’s Multiple comparisons post-hoc test in panel (B).

sec.p: To expand to additional preclinical species, we administered ASO6 in dose-response studies in mice, rats, and NHP and scored the acute inhibition response. As demonstrated previously (Fig. 2), ASO6 had a clear acute inhibition response in mice following ICV injection and in rats following IT administration (Fig. 3B). Like in rats, acute inhibition in NHP after IT administration presents as a loss of spinal reflexes with low doses (4–16 mg in this study). We developed an acute inhibition neurobehavioral scale for NHP (Supplementary Fig. S1C). NHP were dosed weekly with increasing doses of ASO (4, 8, 12, and 16 mg). ASO6 had a dose-dependent acute inhibition response in NHP (Fig. 3B), indicating translation of the acute inhibition response across species following either ICV or IT administration.

sec.title: Acute inhibition is driven by dose level and does not change with repeated administrations
sec.p: Next, we investigated the effect of repeated ASO administration on the acute inhibition response to determine the effect of ASO tissue accumulation or signs of tolerance after repeat dosing. Repeated IT administration in rats with ASO6 showed a consistent 3-h acute inhibition score across all administrations when the dose level was maintained at either 100 or 300 µg (Fig. 4A and B). To determine if this was also true in NHP, the species most relevant for human safety assessments, we again utilized ASO6. In the previous study, a single administration of 4 mg of ASO did not cause an acute inhibition response (Fig. 3B). Here, we administered 6 weekly 4 mg ASO doses, for a total of 24 mg, and there was also no acute inhibition signal observed in the NHP (Fig. 4C and D). Together, these data confirm there is no sensitization with repeated administrations.

caption.p: Acute inhibition responses do not change with chronic ASO accumulation. (A) Experimental design used in panel (B), where rats received three doses of ASO (arrowheads) on days 1, 8, and 15, and acute inhibition was scored on the scale 3 h after each dose (stars). (B) Rats received either 100 or 300 µg of ASO6 weekly via IT administration. (C) Experimental design used in panel (D), where NHPs were dosed with 4 mg of ASO weekly on days 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, and 36 (arrowheads). NHPs were evaluated at 4 h after each dose for acute inhibition (stars), and necropsy performed a week after the last dose on day 43. (D) Spinal reflexes were measured and scored according to the NHP acute inhibition scale. The specific number of animals per group and P value are included in the Supplementary Table S12.

sec.title: Reducing PS backbone modifications mitigates acute inhibition, while commonly used 2′ sugar modifications and divalent cation supplementation do not
sec.p: Next, we determined if chemical modifications contribute to acute inhibition response. PS modifications have been employed in ASO backbones to confer desirable drug-like properties such as increased cellular uptake and metabolic stability [31]. PS modifications are also associated with increased protein binding [13–16]. We hypothesized that the PS modification may be contributing to the acute inhibition response and tested whether it was affected in gapmer ASOs with sugar modifications in the wings that protect the PO backbone from nucleases such that PS is not needed in the wings [32]. We tested two versions of ASO5, a 5-10-5 MOE gapmer targeting mouse Malat1 RNA, one version uniformly modified with the PS modification and another (ASO5_PO) that did not include the 6 PS modifications in the wings (Fig 5A and B; Supplementary Table S1). Both ASO5 and ASO5_PO elicited dose-dependent increases in acute inhibition (Fig. 5C), but the magnitude of response was attenuated with ASO5_PO (Fig. 5C). There was no significant difference in the potency of ASO5 and ASO5_PO in reducing Malat1 RNA in the cortex (Fig. 5D), and a minimal shift in potency in the spinal cord.

caption.p: Reducing PS backbone content mitigates acute inhibition, but 2′ sugar modifications do not. (A) The phosphorothioate (PS) modification replaces a non-binding oxygen on DNA with a sulfur in the phosphate moiety. (B) Phosphodiester (PO) is the naturally occurring phosphate moiety in the backbone of DNA. (C) Dose-response study comparing acute inhibition scores at 3 h post-ICV for ASO5, fully PS-modified backbone (black dots), to ASO5_PO that has the same sequence but contains a mixture of PS and PO in the backbone (orange dots). (D) Dose-response curves 2 weeks post-ICV injection show the potency of a Malat1-targeted ASO fully modified with PS backbone (ASO5) versus a mixed PS/PO backbone (ASO5_PO). ED50 of 18.7% and 95% confidence interval 15.6–22.5 for ASO5 and ED50 of 27.6% and 95% confidence interval 18.7–40.7 for ASO5_PO in the cortex (n = 4). (E) Three-hour acute inhibition scores across multiple ASO sequences synthesized with either full PS (black) or mixed PS/PO (colors) backbone. (F) Three-hour acute inhibition scores for ASO6 sequences with various sugar ring modifications (MOE, LNA, or cEt). Key: backbone modifications for PS indicated by s, and PO is indicated by o. For 2′ sugar modifications, MOE is indicated by E, LNA indicated by L, and cEt indicated by K. Stats for panels (C), (E), and (F) are nonparametric Mann–Whitney test and panel (D) is nonlinear regression (Motulsky). The specific number per group and P value are included in Supplementary Table S13. Each data point represents the mean and error bars represent standard deviations. *P < .05, **P < .01, ***P < .001, ****P < .0001.

sec.p: The same strategy was applied across an additional six 5-10-5 MOE gapmer ASO sequences (ASOs 2–8; Supplementary Table S1), where PS modifications were not included in six linkages in the wings (Supplementary Table S1). Reduction of PS in the backbone conferred a range of reduction in acute inhibition scores 3 h after ICV injection in mice, from complete abolition with ASO2, to highly significant reductions with ASO3 and ASO4, to no significant reduction with ASO8 (Fig. 5E). These results indicate reducing PS content can reduce acute inhibition in most sequences, but not all.

Gapmer ASOs often incorporate either MOE, LNA, or cEt 2′ sugar modifications to improve binding affinity to target RNA sequences [32]. We generated different versions of ASO6, a 5-10-5 20-mer with either five MOE, LNA, or cEt sugar modifications in the 5′ and 3′ wings and either a full PS or a PO/PS mixed phosphate backbone (Fig. 5F and Supplementary Table S1). Mice were injected via ICV with 100 µg ASO, and acute inhibition was quantified at 3 h post-injection. Each of the full PS modified versions elicited acute inhibition scores of 3–4, while scores for each of the mixed PO/PS versions were zero. These data indicate 2′ sugar ring chemistries did not affect acute inhibition in this sequence, but phosphate linkage chemistry can significantly change acute inhibition, regardless of sugar ring modifications.

Previous reports have found divalent cation supplementation in ASO or small interfering RNA (siRNA) dosing solutions can mitigate acute responses [17, 18, 21]. A companion manuscript demonstrates that acute activation phenotypes (i.e. hyperactivity, tremors, etc.) are mitigated by divalent cation supplementation [22], but we find acute inhibition is not affected (Supplementary Results and Supplementary Fig. 4).

sec.title: Acute inhibition response is associated with disruption of neuronal transmission
sec.p: We hypothesized that acute inhibition is caused by blockade of neuronal transmission. To evaluate activity of neural pathways in vivo in rats, we recorded activity of motor and sensory pathways at baseline, 2 h, and 24 h following a 700 µg IT dose of one of five ASOs with a range of acute inhibition scores (0–4). As the acute inhibition response is characterized by loss of motor activity, we first evaluated the full motor circuit from the CNS to the peripheral muscle by quantifying MMEPs following transcranial electrical stimulation of the motor cortex and recording in the right hind paw muscle (Fig. 6A). Consistent with their acute inhibition scores of 0, no suppression of the MMEP occurred with ASOs 2_PO and 3_PO. In contrast, more acutely inhibitory ASOs 4_PO, 7_PO, and 8_PO caused complete reduction of MMEP 2 h post-IT administration. All MMEP recovered by 24 h after dosing.

caption.p: In vivo electrophysiology following IT administration of some ASO sequences shows transient motor pathway inhibition in the CNS. Rats were dosed intrathecally with 700 µg ASO. Lower graphs (A–D) show electrophysiological recordings taken at baseline, 2 h post-ASO dose, and 24 h post-ASO dose. Upper left panels of A–D are schematics of each experimental setup. Upper right panels of A–D are representative traces from ASO8_PO at 2 h post-dose. (A) For MMEPs, stimulation occurred in the motor cortex and motor pathway activity recordings in the hind paw muscle. Graph shows MMEP response at baseline, 2 h post-, and 24 h post-ASO treatment. (B) For SMEPs, stimulation occurred in the motor cortex, and output was recorded in the thoracic (T12) spinal cord corticospinal tract. Graph shows SMEP response at baseline, 2 h post-, and 24 h post-ASO treatment. (C) For HR recordings, stimulation occurred in the tibial nerve and recording in the hind paw muscle. Graph shows H-reflex response at baseline, 2 h post-, and 24 h post-ASO treatment. (D) For SSEPs, stimulation occurred in the tibial nerve and recording in the lumbar spinal cord. Graph shows SSEP response at baseline, 2 h post-, and 24 h post-ASO treatment. The specific number of animals per group and P value are included in Supplementary Table S14. Bars represent the mean, and error bars represent standard deviations. *P < .05, **P < .01, ***P < .001, ****P < .0001 using two-way ANOVA and Dunnett’s post hoc test.

sec.p: To measure the corticospinal motor pathway function within the CNS, the motor cortex was stimulated transcranially, and thoracic SMEPs were measured (Fig. 6B). Again, ASOs 2_PO and 3_PO had no effect, ASO4_PO elicited a partial reduction, and ASOs 7_PO and 8_PO caused a nearly complete reduction in SMEP 2 h post-IT administration, with recovery by 24 h. The severity of SMEP suppression was reflected in the severity of the acute inhibition score for each sequence. These results show clear interruption of neurotransmission in motor pathways.

To evaluate a local lumbar sensorimotor circuit in detail, we measured the HR (a proprioceptive reflex). The tibial nerve was stimulated, which projects to α-motor neurons, which in turn project to the hind paw muscle, where we recorded (Fig. 6C). ASO2_PO and 3_PO had no effect, ASO4_PO and ASOs 7_PO caused a non-statistically significant reduction, and 8_PO caused significant reduction of the HR 2 h post IT administration, with full recovery by 24 h. These results demonstrate acutely inhibitory ASOs interrupt a monosynaptic reflex involving stimulation of sensory fibers, a synapse in the spinal cord, and response in motor neurons.

Finally, to ask whether axonal propagation through sensory fibers was impacted by acute inhibition, somatosensory evoked potentials were measured by stimulating the tibial nerve and recording on the lumbar spinal cord surface (L2–L5) (Fig. 6D). No ASO had any effect at 2 or 24 h after intrathecal dosing on sensory afferent response, indicating intact axonal propagation in the periphery and within the CNS. This is consistent with observations during acute inhibition that when the toes of the animals are pinched, the animals react by abdominal twitching or turning their head towards the stimulus, even if the foot itself may be incapable of moving at the time.

Taken together, the acute inhibition response is likely caused by inhibition of local CNS synapses, rather than by blockade of axonal propagation itself, due to high concentrations of ASOs in the hours post-intrathecal dosing.

sec.title: Acute inhibition response peaks with ASO distribution into the extracellular space and resolves with ASO clearance
sec.p: To examine the kinetics of acute inhibition as they relate to ASO distribution into the parenchyma, intracellular uptake, and clearance, rats were dosed with ASO6 (full PS backbone) or ASO6_PO (mixed PS/PO backbone), and acute inhibition scores were determined prior to necropsy at 1, 3, 6, and 24 h post-IT administration. At each time point, ASO tissue concentration was quantified, and ASO localization was evaluated by anti-ASO immunohistochemical staining. Acute inhibition scores were higher with the full-PS ASO6 than with mixed PS/PO ASO6_PO, with peak inhibition scores at 3–6 h and resolution by 24 h for both compounds (Fig. 7A). ASO concentrations in bulk spinal cord tissue and ASO staining levels were similar for ASO6 and ASO6_PO and followed the same temporal peak as the acute inhibition response at 3–6 h post-IT dose (Fig. 7B and C). By 3 h post-dose in the ventral horn, ASO was localized intracellularly in motor neurons and in the extracellular space surrounding them (Fig. 7D). By 24 h, ASO bulk tissue concentrations were reduced (Fig. 7B), and ASO staining showed clearance from the extracellular space with any CNS-retained ASO localized mostly intracellularly (Fig. 7D insets). These data indicate a matched temporal evolution of ASO distribution to the parenchyma, intracellular uptake, and extracellular clearance with the peak and resolution of acute inhibition response.

caption.p: Acute inhibition responses resolve with ASO clearance and cellular internalization. (A) Time course of acute inhibition responses in rats injected intrathecally with either a fully-PS modified version (ASO6) or a mixed PS/6PO backbone version (ASO6_PO; Supplementary Table S1) of the same ASO sequence. (B) ASO concentration over time in the spinal cord (SC). (C) ASO staining in the ventral horn of the spinal cord shows ASO distribution. (D) Zoomed-in image of ASO staining at 3 h post-dosing (left panels) and 24 h (middle panels; inset of staining in motor neurons in right panels). The specific number of animals per group and P value are included in Supplementary Table S15. Each data point represents the mean, error bars represent standard deviations, and *P < .05, **P < .01, ***P < .001, ****P < .0001. Stats for panels (A) and (B) using nonparametric Mann–Whitney test.

sec.title: ASOs that cause acute inhibition in vivo also suppress spontaneous field potentials in primary cortical cultures
sec.p: To further investigate underlying mechanisms of acute inhibition, we established an in vitro model using MEA recordings of spontaneous field potentials in primary mouse cortical cultures, an assay routinely used to explore neurotoxicity of drug compounds [33]. Three ASOs with a range of acute inhibition responses from 0 to 7 after a 300 µg ICV injection in mice were tested at different concentrations in the cultures. The ASOs caused network firing suppression relative to baseline in a dose-dependent manner that reflected the severity of ASOs’ in vivo acute inhibition scores (Supplementary Fig. S5A). Using this information, we selected a single in vivo dose level (300 µg) and an in vitro concentration level (50 µM) and tested a panel of 33 gapmer ASOs (Supplementary Table S3) of varying lengths and chemistries, including wing MOE, LNA, and cEt sugar modifications that are often used ASO designs [34, 35]. The in vivo acute inhibition scores were highly correlated with the level of firing inhibition (r = 0.84; Supplementary Fig. S5B), indicating the in vitro assay captured the degree of acute inhibition of a particular sequence, regardless of chemistry.

To identify ASOs with the lowest potential for acute inhibition, we selected a different panel of 34 ASOs (Supplementary Table S2), mostly designed with lower PS content than those above, and increased the dose at which we evaluated acute inhibition in vivo to 700 µg. We also increased the concentration at which we tested the ASOs in vitro to 120 µM, based on a concentration-ranging study with several representative PS/PO ASOs (Supplementary Fig. S5C). Again, we saw a strong correlation between the in vitro and in vivo response (r = 0.9; Fig. 8A and B). We find that screening PS/PO ASOs in this in vitro system at 120 µM and selecting compounds with <60% inhibition of baseline firing rate should identify ASOs with little risk for severe acute inhibition at 700 µg in mice, which is equivalent to the human dose of 2450 mg (based on CSF scaling [36]) and should provide wide safety margins compared to typical clinical doses.

caption.p: In vivo ASO-mediated inhibition scores correlate with inhibition of neuronal firing in vitro and are reversible upon washout. (A) Primary neurons treated with MOE gapmer ASOs at 120 µM concentration compared to the 3 h acute inhibition scores. (B) Representative raster plots of neuronal spike patterns at baseline and after treatment with 120 µM of ASO2_PO (acute inhibition score = 0) and ASO8_PO (acute inhibition score = 7). (C) Schematic of experimental design. (D) Table ASOs used in panels (E) and (F) with the corresponding in vivo acute inhibition score following 700 µg ICV injection in mice. (E) Representative raster plots showing primary neural culture firing at baseline, after treatment with tetrodotoxin (TTX) (positive control), or after treatment with ASO42 and ASO39, which have an in vivo 3 h acute inhibition score of 7. (F) MEA firing rates after treatment with ASO50, ASO48, ASO40, and ASO42 (black bars), and following washout of the ASOs at 10 min, 1 h, and 2 h post-treatment (white bars). The specific number of animals per group and P value are included in Supplementary Tables S16 and S17. Each data point represents the mean; error bars represent standard deviations, and *P < .05, **P < .01, ***P < .001, ****P < .0001. Stats for panel (F): two-way ANOVA and Šídák’s post hoc test.

sec.title: Suppression of spontaneous firing is reversed by removal of ASO from culture media
sec.p: The kinetics of ASO distribution and clearance following CNS administration, combined with the temporal evolution of the acute inhibition response in vivo, suggest that ASO in the extracellular space is potentially responsible for the inhibition of neuronal firing. To test this directly, we asked if ASO-mediated inhibition of spontaneous firing in vitro would be resolved by removing the ASO from the media and thus from the extracellular space. We applied either media or a panel of ASOs with different levels of in vivo acute inhibition to the primary cultures and recorded for 5 min at baseline, during ASO treatment, and after washout of ASO from the culture media (Fig. 8C and D). As before, the level of in vitro firing rate suppression (Fig. 8E and F) reflected the severity of the in vivo acute inhibition score (Fig. 8D). Following washout, firing rates recovered for all ASOs, and no differences were observed amongst treatment groups, even after incubation with ASO for up to 2 h prior to washout (Fig. 8F). These results indicate that the inhibitory effect of ASO fully reversed with removal of ASO from the extracellular space.

sec.title: ASO-mediated suppression of neuronal firing can be overcome by any excitatory stimulus
sec.p: To further exclude axonal propagation as causal for acute inhibition response and to determine whether a single receptor or pathway is involved, we applied various neurotransmitters, excitatory agonists, or inhibitory antagonists in dose response during ASO treatment in primary neural cultures and recorded spontaneous field potentials via MEA. First, in a positive control experiment, TTX was used to inhibit axonal propagation via blockade of voltage-gated Na+ channels. About 90% inhibition of firing was observed, and no neurotransmitter, agonist, or antagonist was able to rescue the firing (Supplementary Fig. S6), as is expected if axonal propagation is inhibited. In contrast, ASO8_PO (acute inhibition score = 7 at 700 µg via ICV in mice) inhibited firing by 85%–90%, which was fully rescued with 100 µM glutamate or 50 µM acetylcholine and partially rescued by N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA), α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA), or bicuculline (Fig 9A–E). ASO7_PO (acute inhibition score = 4 at 700 µg via ICV in mice) inhibited firing by 60%, which was fully rescued by 50 µM acetylcholine, 50 µM glutamate, 25 µM NMDA, 1 µM AMPA, or 25 µM bicuculline (Fig. 9A–E). ASO2_PO (acute inhibition score = 0 at 700 µg via ICV in mice) did not result in firing inhibition (Fig. 9A–E). As expected, in non-ASO conditions, application of these agents dose-responsively increased firing before inhibiting activity at very high doses (right panel, Fig. 9A-E) [37]. These results show ASO-mediated inhibition of neuronal activity could be partially or fully rescued via modulation of any excitatory or inhibitory cues at receptors present in the post-synaptic density. This suggests that ASO likely blocks firing by non-specific protein binding in the synapse but does not inhibit action potential propagation.

caption.p: Excitatory agonists and inhibitory antagonists partially or fully rescue ASO-mediated inhibition of neuronal firing. (A–E) Primary cultures were treated with various agonists or antagonists in a dose response alone (far right panels) or in combination with ASO8_PO, ASO7_PO, and ASO2_PO that cause an acute inhibition score of 7, 4, and 0, respectively. Accordingly, ASO8_PO, ASO7_PO, and ASO2_PO caused severe, moderate, and no inhibition in in vitro spike rates, respectively. (A) Glutamate (Glu) or (B) Acetylcholine (Ach) concentrations between 5 and 100 µM fully rescued any ASO-mediated inhibition of firing. (C) NMDA, (D) AMPA, and (E) Bicuculline methiodide (BIC) fully rescued moderate inhibition of firing caused by ASO7_PO, but only partially rescued the severe suppression caused by ASO8_PO. The specific number of replicates and P values are included in Supplementary Tables S18–S22. Each data point represents the mean, error bars represent standard deviations, and *P < .05, **P < .01, ***P < .001, ****P < .0001. Stats for panels (A–E): two-way ANOVA and Šídák’s post hoc test.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Here, we characterize a class of neurobehavioral responses following delivery of ASOs to the CNS that reflect inhibition of neuronal activity, including loss of lower spinal reflexes, hypoactivity, lethargy, paresis, sedation, and ataxia. We describe how the acute inhibition response presents differently when the ASO is delivered through either IT or ICV routes due to differential local CNS tissue concentrations of ASO. In preclinical species, we provide a standardized method for capturing this acute inhibition response in scales that can be easily adapted to the drug discovery pipeline. These findings translate across species, allowing for screening paradigms that can identify ASOs that do not exhibit acute inhibition at therapeutic doses. The acute inhibition response peaks around 3 h post-administration and is typically fully reversible by 24 h post-dose, with no identifiable sequelae.

Our data support a model where the acute inhibition response is caused by inhibition of synaptic transmission due to high extracellular concentrations of phosphorothioate ASO. The transient nature of the response is coincident with the clearance of ASO out of the extracellular space and into uptake into cells. Acute inhibition is a hybridization-independent effect that is sequence dependent and can be mitigated by decreasing phosphorothioate content and avoiding G-rich sequences.

It should be noted that, in addition to loss of spinal reflexes in NHP reported here, a wider range of transient, acute inhibition responses presenting in the hours after IT ASO administration can occur [20]. These can include signs such as knuckling (deficits in proprioception positioning manifesting as walking on the digits or knuckles of the hind limbs), ataxia (inability of the truncal, pelvic, and limb muscles to move in unison, creating an unsteady gait), and limb paresis (loss of weight-bearing ability or movement of any limb), and are assessed as a part of standard neurological exams performed post-IT administration of ASOs. These are likely part of the same acute inhibition response, but the ASO sequences and doses used in the NHP studies reported herein were not sufficient to elicit these more severe responses.

The acute inhibition response is mechanistically distinct from the acute activation response characterized in our companion manuscript [22]. The acute activation response can include seizures and hyperactivity and occurs within the first minutes to 1 h following administration with resolution 2–4 h after dosing [17, 18, 22], highlighting an important temporal difference in the two acute responses. Unlike the acute inhibition response, the acute activation response is mitigated with cation supplementation, occurs with both ASOs and siRNAs, and is not dependent on PS content [22]. Taken together, to identify safe oligonucleotides for clinical use, our data support evaluating both classes of responses immediately after dosing, at 3 h after dosing, as well as at 24 h post-dose to ensure an evaluation of all potential acute responses as well as reversibility.

Our work extends earlier efforts to understand chemical contributions and establishes that the severity of acute inhibition is dependent on the sequence and backbone chemistry of the ASO, but not the 2′ sugar modifications (either MOE, LNA, or cEt), though sugar modifications have been reported elsewhere to affect acute responses [21]. ASOs with identical chemical motifs but different sequences exhibited a wide range of acute inhibition levels. We found in vivo acute inhibition severity was positively associated with enrichment for guanine (G) nucleotides. A previous report also reported a positive association with G-rich sequences in an in vitro assay of ASO-mediated suppression of synchronous neuronal activity [19]. With that said, the association of G-rich sequences with acute inhibition is a general observation across thousands of ASO sequences, and not every ASO sequence will follow this rule; a prime example is in Fig. 4, where ASO-4, -5, and -8 sequences contain equal G content (Supplementary Table S1) but have vastly different acute inhibition responses. Additionally, though present, we did not find a strong negative association between in vivo acute inhibition and adenosine (A)-rich sequences, as had been reported in the in vitro assay [19]. Together, this underlines the importance of empirically testing clinical candidate ASOs for the acute inhibition response. We also found replacement of PS linkages with PO in the wings of a gapmer ASO did not profoundly affect the ED50 of target RNA knockdown but did mitigate acute inhibition in most sequences, indicating this can be an approach to improving tolerability of ASOs without affecting efficacy.

In vivo electrophysiological recordings demonstrated that ASOs causing acute inhibition interrupt neurotransmission of cortical and spinal motor neurons 2 h post-dosing. Evoked responses were dampened or fully blocked in motor pathways either within the CNS or from the CNS to the periphery, while axonal propagation through sensory pathways from the periphery into the CNS remained intact. That axonal propagation is not inhibited by ASO is also supported in MEA experiments showing any excitatory stimuli could overcome ASO-mediated neuronal inhibition but could not overcome TTX-mediated blockade of axonal propagation. Whether the inhibition of neurotransmission is pre- or post-synaptic or both remains unclear and should be tested in future experiments. Altogether, after IT administration, this points to local inhibition of spinal cord synapses, likely caused by high extracellular concentrations of ASOs present acutely after dosing. Indeed, ASO concentrations in the spinal cord peak between 1 and 3 h post-IT administration, coincident with the peak of acute inhibition response. ASO concentrations clear between 6 and 24 h post-dose, coincident with the reversal of acute inhibition.

We modeled acute inhibition in primary cortical cultures by measuring spontaneous activity via MEA. The severity of neuronal activity suppression in culture was highly correlated to the severity of the in vivo acute inhibition scores. The fast onset of neuronal firing suppression in the minutes after ASO application and reversal in the minutes after washout in vitro suggests acute inhibition is likely mediated at the extracellular level rather than by mechanisms involving cellular uptake and intracellular trafficking. Others have also demonstrated reduced activity in a spontaneous calcium oscillation in vitro assay following application of ASO and reduced intracellular calcium levels in rat primary neurons [17]. These results are consistent with, and likely secondary to, the suppression of synaptic neuronal activity that we have observed, rather than a direct effect on intracellular calcium dynamics. It is also unclear whether the ASOs used in the published assays were acutely inhibitory or activating (or both). Our data set expands upon the previous work with a significantly larger range of chemistries and sequences and additional mechanistic insights. We show that in vivo acute inhibition responses are predicted by in vitro firing suppression, and that firing suppression can be quickly ameliorated by washout of ASO from the extracellular space.

We also demonstrate that the inhibition of neuronal firing can be partially or fully overcome by adding any number of excitatory cues (glutamate, acetylcholine, etc.), indicating it is likely not mediated by ASO interaction with any one specific class of receptor. It is possible that ASOs causing acute inhibition instead bind multiple receptors in the post-synaptic density or prevent presynaptic release of neurotransmitters. Phosphorothioate ASOs can bind a wide range of proteins, with the extent of binding correlated to the phosphorothioate content [13–16]. Since phosphorothioate content also correlates with the acute inhibition response, it follows that acute inhibition could be mediated by ASO-protein interactions in the synaptic cleft. Future investigations could explore whether acutely inhibitory ASOs more tightly bind specific proteins or are more promiscuous binders, or whether supplementing dosing solutions with protein content might mitigate acute inhibition responses. We have also confirmed that the acute inhibition response does not correlate with CSF neurotransmitter or glucose levels (data not shown). Others have also ruled out innate immune activation as causative for any acute phenotype [21]. Given the rapid kinetics and the reversibility of the acute inhibition response in the minutes following washout of ASO in in vitro studies, it is also unlikely that hybridization events contribute. Understanding these exact mechanisms and the synaptic components involved will be important for identifying solutions that can mitigate this response for all ASO sequences.

As ASOs continue to advance as an important modality for treating neurological diseases, future work is needed to apply these learnings as we continue to refine ASO chemistry and design. Ultimately, sustained efforts to further understand ASO safety will be key to realizing the full potential of ASOs in the CNS and to ensure patients receive treatments that are both safe and effective.
